state_background_check.value: No — Tennessee's eligibility statute (Tenn. Code Ann. § 8-18-101) applies only to persons "qualified to hold office under the authority of this state" by its own text, not federal office; separately, the U.S. Constitution's own qualifications for Congress (age, citizenship, residency) can't be added to by any state, so this doesn't reach U.S. House or Senate candidates either way
state_background_check.snippet: Tenn. Code Ann. § 8-18-101: "All persons eighteen (18) years of age or older who are citizens of the United States and of this state... are qualified to hold office under the authority of this state except: (1) Those who have been convicted of offering or giving a bribe, or any other offense declared infamous under § 40-20-112..." Congressional qualifications are set exclusively by the U.S. Constitution, confirmed per https://www.everycrsreport.com/reports/R41946.html: "the Framers intended the Constitution to be the exclusive source of qualifications for Members of Congress, and that the Framers thereby 'divested' States of any power to add qualifications."

platform.value: Health care is a human right; fight to expand Medicaid in Tennessee to cover 300,000 people without coverage and prevent rural hospital closures
platform.snippet: Two rural hospitals in District 3 have already closed. Nine more are at risk. Tennessee is one of ten states still refusing to expand Medicaid, leaving 300,000 people without coverage. Health care is a human right — and this district deserves a representative who will fight for it – because lives depend on it.
